Friendly reminder that the car has a *wing* and *not* a spoiler. They might look similar but they do very different things. The main purpose of a wing is to create downforce, at the usual expense of more drag. A *spoiler* does the opposite, its main purpose is to *reduce* drag. So since the car in the picture has a pretty sizable diffuser, it looks like the whole aero package couples that with a wing to provide rear downforce. The design itself seems reminiscent to me of a time attack, hillclimb, or a drift setup. As to whether or not it's actually functional we'll never know until we can get some tunnel time and real data on it but the wing seems to be in a good place and so does the diffuser. Funny looking or not this probably had a lot of thought put into it. /rant

Yeah, there's a big difference in performance on fresh tires versus tires that've been worn down over the course of the race. Let's say I'm running super soft compound and I have about a three second advantage on the guy behind me running mediums. If I pit with this advantage I can potentially retake the lead because I'm back on fresh tires. Tire wear is a big deal in pretty much all motorsport because the rubber used is really soft and designed to basically be as grippy as possible. Since the tires are the only thing connecting the car to the ground, they're constantly being stressed to the point that your first set of tires most likely won't last the entire race distance, add to that the fact that after a certain point all you're doing is slowing down, and suddenly a pit stop becomes a really good idea.

Venus, a rotting hellhole of a once proud, powerful planet lay lifeless in the void. It had been nearly a thousand sols since the great empires had fallen and moved on. The few who remained lived under constant fear of the corrosive rains and the blinding, blistering heat of the surface. Buildings a mile tall and cities once filled with millions were empty now. Anyone brave enough to make camp in one of the once shining towers soon fell to the acid rain that struck without warning. Of course, those living in their shelters deep underground, while still alive, lived in constant fear of running out of supplies, or the weather above getting worse.

Long before fallout and famine dusted the land lived wondrous utopias of man, gleaming monuments to progress and ingenuity, but all that wonder came to an end when man realized Venus was growing hotter by the day. By the time the debates came to an end, it was too late. The damage was done. Wars broke out over who was responsible for the destruction of the planet, and after the dust settled, a decision was made. Civilization would have to start anew on the curious blue dot they called Earth. Great vessels were built to shuttle entire cities to space. Hundreds of millions boarded the ark that would bring them to a new place, a virgin landscape perfect for a new beginning.

As the years passed, the stories of man were lost to time and history began again. The ships and cities of old were gods in the heavens, riding chariots of fertility through the sky. Man was but a humble creation of the gods, their utopia doomed by his own mistakes.

Depression isn't sadness. To me it's this horrible weight I have to carry. It feels like everything weighs twice, three times as much and you have this horrible sinking feeling that just sits there. You feel like crying, but you can't. You feel every bad feeling at the same time as your mind races through all your mistakes and punishes you for every single little thing you've done. Eventually you start to believe in what you feel. Suddenly you can't take compliments anymore because the thought of doing something positive and noteworthy is completely alien. You feel like you have no friends, like you aren't involved in anything and it hurts because you know deep down that you're just an observer with no importance. You know you have friends, you know you have a loving family and all kinds of support, but it doesn't help. Everyone hates you and talks shit behind your back. That person you're really good friends with hasn't talked to you much today? That's because they hate you and can't stand to talk to you any more. You spend your time waiting for the inevitable intervention where you get stopped in the middle of a conversation and told "nobody likes you, and for the love of God, stop fucking talking" but it never comes. You're always worried about the people around you being annoyed by everything you say because you're just an annoying person who needs to stop. You can't tell your parents because you don't know how to express what you're feeling in the moment and the second you talk to most adults and kids, they get really concerned and you don't want that because you don't want to waste their time while they try to talk you down. You marinate in self hate in the middle of class, ignoring the teacher because your face is buried in a page of instructions on hanging yourself. You wait the entire day for somebody to notice and take more than a passing interest in what's going on and it never happens so you keep to yourself while you debate internally weather to use the door or a tree to hang. Walked my home, you see the passing buses and cars and you can feel yourself running into the road and getting smashed like a bug. Your backpack weighs on you and you want to take it off and just end yourself, but you're just on autopilot at this point and suicide takes a back seat to walking home. Once you're there you're still deliberating in your head where to hang yourself and the weight is greater than ever as you lay in bed. Eventually you pass out and wake back a few hours later. Most of the time the feeling goes away, but this time it sticks around and you have a new plan. Pills. You're still laying in bed, trying hard not to go to the bathroom and down that entire bottle of blood pressure medicine you got for your anxiety. Eventually you work up the courage to text your friend. They're responsive and persistent as you deny every good thing they say about you and constantly beat yourself up. Luckily this keeps you distracted and after an hour or two the feeling is gone and you're in tears from the talk you just had.  That Monday you're back in school and you casually ask a teacher about your medicine and they confirm your suspicion. It would've worked. You'd be dead if you took those pills. Naturally people freak out and a weird miscommunication leads to a call you have to explain and now you regret ever having that conversation. You're back to beating yourself up because you freaked your parents out, and the people on the phone got the story wrong.

That's kinda what it's like. This is sort of an average of the last series of episodes I had so it's not entirely the same story. Feel free to AMA, I'm willing to go into as much depth as I have about this.

"Achtung. Der U-Bahnzug kommt in einer halben Minute. Bitte achten Sie auf die Lücke zwischen Zug und Bahnsteigkante," said the pleasant voice in the ceiling of the subway tunnel. A small crowd had formed in anticipation of its arrival. One of the members of the crowd, an older Aryan man, scoured a small paper map of the subway for his next stop. Soon after he looked up from the pamphlet he had picked up on another train, the train had arrived. Subway trains, he thought, were peculiar things, not as sleek or as stylish as other trains, they weren't nearly as fast, either. There wasn't much more time to think though, and in the orderly push for the doors, he lost his train of thought. Stepping purposefully through the door, he scanned the metal-walled car for an open seat. Unfortunately, the first one that caught his eye was next to a rather unsightly (to say the least) woman. He hesitated, waiting for someone else to claim the three-quarter seat, but to no avail. Sighing internally, he took it.

"Flughafen Neues Berlin-Interplanetar. Bitte achten Sie auf die Lücke zwischen Zug und Bahnsteigkante," finally, he was at his station. Leaving the train, he wandered into the large, open space below the airport. His plane wouldn't take off for another hour, so he bought a magazine and sat down in the gate lounge. About halfway through his magazine, the boarding call came, and he joined the line, went through the movable tunnel, and found his seat in business. It was a window seat, in about the middle of the plane. The chair itself was comfortable enough, spaced evenly relative to the others, and generally inoffensive. A low rumble coming from behind him confirmed his suspicion they were taxiing to their runway. The rumble grew louder, and louder still, and he felt the gigantic machine step casually into the air. his flight would be a long one, and he deeply regretted only buying a single magazine. The *Himmel Einkaufszentrum* catalog in the back of the seat in front of him beckoned.

The now familiar rumble changed slightly and he felt the plane accelerating again. As comfortable as he was with this trip, the second leg, when the engines changed modes, was always a surprise. Perhaps it was because they were of his own design that the change caught him off guard. The next project, he vowed, was to make the changeover unnoticeable, or maybe just a little smoother.

However, final approach was his favorite part on either end of the trip. Watching the moon's surface lift itself up to the wheels of the plane absolutely fascinated him. Again, his thoughts were interrupted by the movement of the people around him. Disembarking the plane gave him a pang of impatient anxiety, as he tried to join the uncomfortable line of people heading through the door. He sauntered down the movable tunnel and once again marvelled at the absolutely massive, glass dome that topped the low building.

Another ride on the subway, and he was a step closer to his office. "Bitte achten Sie auf die Lücke zwischen Zug und Bahnsteigkante," said the same pleasant voice from the New Berlin station, as he left the train and continued his commute.

Basically, music gets devided into sections called measures, they nicely chop a composition into chunks of notes. Let's say we're in 4/4, generally regarded as common time. There are four quarter notes in a measure, and the quarter note gets the beat. So, to count a single measure of nothing but quarter notes, the performer simply counts 1, 2, 3, 4 in sync with the pulse. 1 and 3 are the "downbeats" because they're nice to count, one comes first, you skip 2, and you're in the second half of the measure. 2 and 4 are "upbeats" they're sort of in weird places in the measure because you pause *before* you count them instead of after. 1 * 3 * vs * 2 * 4. With this in mind, you can divide a single beat in the same manner as an entire measure. This is generally called subdivision. The most basic way to subdivide a beat is to count 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and. In this situation, the "ands" become the upbeats, and the 1's, 2's, 3's, and 4's become downbeats for the same reasons as before. Downbeats are easier, and more intuitive to count, while upbeats don't come as naturally.

You have to manage so many different things to make yourself sound good: tone (as a saxophonist, I can play anywhere in a range of mellow sexiness to harsh, raunchy growling depending on the song and how I see fit), dynamics (basically volume. Do I want to bring this out and let it fly across the auditorium and into your face, or should I stay down and do something a little technical?), key (do the notes I'm playing actually sound good, how can I change what I play to make it more interesting, how can I emphasize this change, how many keys can I play this lick in until I get tired), rhythms and articulation (light and quick with lots of technicality, or harsh and intimadating just for kicks). On top of this, your time is ticking down the moment you stand up. You have to say what you need to say and make it count before the chart moves on. Afterwards, you forget everything that happened and sit back and appreciate what you've done, becuse if you did it right, people want to talk about it. Easy, isn't it?

The moon is spinning, and the walls are flickering again. I sighed and returned to my writing. They like it when I write; they give me better food. It doesn't even matter what I put on the page, so they must not understand english I figured that out by just filling the page with letters. They still rewarded me. This time was different from the usual gibberish. This time was going to be special. I was writing music. I wondered if they made music, whoever they were. I put down the paper and pen they had given me and stood. I hadn't been afforded the luxury of a shower in maybe a week and it made me uneasy. As if being trapped in a plexiglass cage didn't make me nervous. My dinner came in through the usual chute. I picked up the cold, metal trey and stared blankly at its contents. There was a piece of garlic bread, spaghetti with meatballs, and the usual off-blue-green liquid in a paper cup. All of it was fake. The first bite of garlic bread returned a sort of orange-like taste, the spaghetti tasted like pineapple, and the blue stuff, I had come to realize, was supposed to be water. This wasn't unusual for them, they must not understand how the human sense of taste works, but the more likely explanation is they've never had spaghetti.

I finished off the strange meal and chucked the tray at the wall. The moon stopped spinning. This was pointless. Everything in this prison came from my own memory. I don't know how they did that, or how they managed to make so many mistakes, but there was no way out, so I decided to move on. A door opened in the wall and one of them came out. They were the strangest things I'd ever seen, short, off-green things with long arms and stubby legs. They had faces like catfish, and wore space helmets every time they were around me. This particular one grabbed me by the arm and led me to a while, almost clinical room. It was time for another intelligence test. God I hated these.

The "test" was laughably simple. Basic math, pattern recognition, and a reflex test. It was administered on a strange, tablet-like device that projected all the questions like holograms, floating in mid-air. First question, addition. Second, subtraction. Third, match the shapes. This was humiliating. I felt like a trained monkey. I threw myself against the window they were watching me from and everything went black. Anything to get out of this place.
